title: Narrowing, unions, and why not enums
objectives: Narrow a union with `typeof`, `in`, `instanceof` and equality checks, including the `typeof null === "object"` trap
Write a type guard for `unknown` data, and explain that TypeScript trusts a predicate without checking it
Model states as a discriminated union, with a `never` check that turns a newly added case into a compile error
Choose a union or an `as const` object (checked with `satisfies`) over an `enum`, citing enums' runtime objects, `isolatedModules`, TS 5.8 `erasableSyntaxOnly` and Node type stripping

sources.title: TypeScript 4.9 release notes: satisfies, and in narrowing
TypeScript 5.0 release notes: all enums are union enums

questions.prompt: `if (typeof value === "object") return Object.keys(value);` — written in plain JavaScript, which input still crashes it?

options.text: `null`
`new Date()`
`"text"`

questions.explanation: `typeof null` is `"object"` — a historical accident JavaScript keeps for compatibility — so `null` enters the branch and `Object.keys(null)` throws. Arrays and dates are objects and work (`[]` gives `[]`); a string never enters the branch. In TypeScript the narrowed type is `object | null`, which is why the compiler rejects this line until you add `value !== null`.

questions.prompt: Under `strict`, `catch (err)` gives `err: unknown`. Which check lets you read `err.message` safely?

options.text: `if (err instanceof Error)`
`if (typeof err === "Error")`
`if ("message" in err)`
`const e = err as Error;`

questions.explanation: `instanceof` narrows to the class, and it's a real runtime check. `typeof` only ever returns primitive type names plus `"object"` and `"function"`, so `"Error"` never matches (TypeScript flags the comparison). `in` doesn't compile on `unknown`, and at runtime it throws a `TypeError` when someone throws a string. A cast checks nothing — a thrown string has no `message`.

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript verify about `function isUser(x: unknown): x is User { return true; }`?

options.text: Only that it returns a boolean — every caller will narrow to `User`, whatever the body checks
That the body tests every property of `User`
It generates runtime validation from the `User` type
It's a compile error: a type guard must check something

questions.explanation: A type predicate is an assertion you make, like `as`: TypeScript trusts it and narrows at every call site. Types are erased, so nothing is generated at runtime either. A guard that checks too little (one key, not its type) makes bad data look typed — test guards like any other code, or derive the type from a schema library's check.

questions.prompt: Which type makes "loading **and** failed at the same time" impossible to represent?

options.text: `{ status: "loading" } | { status: "success"; data: Order[] } | { status: "error"; error: string }`
`{ loading: boolean; data?: Order[]; error?: string }`
`{ status: string; data?: Order[]; error?: string }`
`{ isLoading: boolean; isError: boolean; data: Order[] | null }`

questions.explanation: A discriminated union lists the states that exist, each with its own fields, so `data` exists only on success and `error` only on error. The bag of optionals allows `{ loading: true, error: "…" }`; a free-form `status: string` can't be narrowed at all; and two booleans give four combinations for three states. Checking `state.status` narrows to exactly one member.

questions.prompt: You add `{ kind: "refunded" }` to the `Payment` union. What does `const unhandled: never = payment;` in a switch's `default` branch do?

options.text: Every switch that doesn't handle `"refunded"` stops compiling, at that line
Throws at runtime when a refunded payment reaches the `default`
Nothing — `never` accepts any value
TypeScript generates the missing `case` for you

questions.explanation: When every member is handled, the narrowed type in `default` is `never`, so the assignment compiles. An unhandled member is left over, and it isn't assignable to `never`: `Type '{ kind: "refunded" }' is not assignable to type 'never'`. The assignment itself does nothing at runtime — add a `throw` after it for data that slips past the types. And it's the other way round: nothing is assignable *to* `never`.

questions.prompt: Your team starts running `.ts` files directly with Node's built-in type stripping and turns on TS 5.8's `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Which declaration has to change?

options.text: `enum Role { Admin = "admin", Viewer = "viewer" }`
`type Role = "admin" | "viewer";`
`const Role = { Admin: "admin", Viewer: "viewer" } as const;`
`interface User { role: Role }`

questions.explanation: Type stripping runs TypeScript by deleting the types — but an `enum` isn't only a type, it compiles to a runtime object, so it can't be deleted. Node rejects the file (`ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`), and `erasableSyntaxOnly` reports the same thing at compile time. Type aliases and interfaces are erased; an `as const` object is plain JavaScript plus an erasable assertion.

questions.prompt: A library's `.d.ts` declares `export declare const enum Level { Low = 1, High = 2 }`. In your app, with `isolatedModules` on, you write `Level.Low`. What happens?

options.text: Compile error: `Cannot access ambient const enums when 'isolatedModules' is enabled`
It compiles, and `Level.Low` is inlined as `1`
It compiles to a property read on the library's `Level` object
It compiles, then throws at runtime because `Level` is undefined

questions.explanation: Inlining a `const enum` needs its values, and under `isolatedModules` each file must be compilable alone — a single-file transpiler can't read another package's `.d.ts`. So TypeScript makes it an error to reference an ambient const enum. Without `isolatedModules`, `tsc` would inline `1` — and could inline a value from a different version of the library than the one that runs, which is one of the handbook's const-enum pitfalls.

questions.prompt: `const routes: Record<string, string | ((id: string) => string)> = { home: "/", user: (id: string) => "/u/" + id };` — then `routes.user("7")` fails to compile. What fixes it while still checking the object?

options.text: Replace the annotation with `{ … } satisfies Record<string, string | ((id: string) => string)>`
Replace the annotation with `{ … } as Record<string, string | ((id: string) => string)>`
Call it as `routes.user!("7")`
Add `as const` and keep the annotation

questions.explanation: An annotation checks the value and then *replaces* its type, so `routes.user` becomes `string | function`, which isn't callable. `satisfies` (TS 4.9+) checks the same constraint but keeps the inferred type, so `user` stays a function. `as` keeps the same widened type (and checks less). `!` only removes `null`/`undefined`. With the annotation still in place, `as const` changes nothing about the declared type.

prompts.prompt: Narrow `input: string | number` to a string before calling a string method.
prompts.explanation: `typeof` returns a type-name string at runtime, and TypeScript narrows on the comparison. Inside the `if`, `input` is `string`; after it returns, the rest of the function sees `number`.

prompts.prompt: Write a type guard for `unknown` input: rule out `null`, then prove `id` exists and is a string.
code: return typeof x === "object" && x ___ null && "id" in x && typeof x.id === "string";
prompts.explanation: `x is Order` is the type predicate that makes callers narrow. `typeof null` is `"object"`, so `x !== null` is required before `in`, which throws on `null` at runtime. (A real guard checks every field it promises — TypeScript won't.)

prompts.prompt: Make the `default` branch a compile error whenever a `Shape` member isn't handled — and a loud failure at runtime.
prompts.explanation: If every member was handled, `shape` is `never` here and the assignment compiles; a new member makes it an error at this line. The `throw` covers what the types can't: values from outside that carry a `kind` the code has never seen.

prompts.prompt: Declare the roles once, as a readonly tuple of literals, and derive the union type from it.
prompts.explanation: `as const` keeps each element's literal type (otherwise the array is `string[]`). Indexing the tuple type with `number` gives the union of its element types: `"admin" | "editor" | "viewer"`. The array still exists at runtime for dropdowns and validation; no enum needed.

prompts.prompt: Check that the label map covers every `Status` key (here `"open" | "shipped"`) while the object keeps its own inferred type, instead of taking a declared one.
prompts.code: const LABELS = { open: "Open", shipped: "Shipped" } ___ Record<Status, string>;
prompts.explanation: `satisfies` (TS 4.9+) reports a missing or misspelled key — so adding a member to `Status` breaks every map that lacks it — while the object keeps its own inferred type rather than the checked one. The string values still widen to `string`; `as const satisfies` keeps them as readonly literals.

snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: An enum is a real object at runtime, and a numeric enum stores both directions: `Direction.Up === 0` and `Direction[0] === "Up"`. So it has four keys, and integer-like keys come first. Code that loops over an enum to build a dropdown shows `0` and `1` as options. String enums have no reverse mapping; an `as const` object has exactly the keys you wrote.

snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: `typeof null` is `"object"` (a bug from JavaScript's first version, kept for compatibility), and arrays are objects too. So `typeof x === "object"` alone admits `null` and arrays. Add `x !== null`, and `!Array.isArray(x)` if arrays aren't welcome.

code: type Money = { amount: number; currency: string };
function isMoney(x: unknown): x is Money {
return typeof x === "object" && x !== null && "amount" in x;
snippets.question: It compiles under `strict`. What is logged?
snippets.explanation: The guard checks that `amount` exists, not that it's a number, and TypeScript believes its `x is Money` claim. So `body.amount` is typed `number` while holding the string `"12"`, and `"12" + 1` concatenates to `"121"`. Add `typeof x.amount === "number"` — a guard must prove everything its predicate promises.
